claims.text: A controlled heat treatment can induce short-range ordering of Cr atoms in high-chromium steel.
Induced short-range ordering produces a more uniform Cr distribution.
A more uniform Cr distribution promotes formation of a continuous Cr-rich passive oxide film.
The resulting Cr-rich passive oxide film is self-healing.
The continuous, self-healing Cr-rich passive film significantly improves corrosion resistance.
Short-range ordering forms Cr-rich nanoclusters in the steel microstructure.
Short-range-ordered Cr-rich nanoclusters nucleate a uniform protective chromium oxide layer.
Short-range ordering minimizes Cr-depleted sites by homogenizing the Cr distribution.
Minimizing Cr-depleted sites causes the passive film to form more rapidly and consistently.
Self-healing of the passive film under mild disturbances enhances resistance to localized and generalized corrosion.
Heat-treated samples will passivate faster than untreated samples.
Heat-treated samples will develop fewer local corrosion pits than untreated samples.
Heat-treated samples will have a lower overall corrosion rate than untreated samples.
Standard-processed control samples have a more heterogeneous Cr distribution than tailored heat-treated samples.
The heterogeneous Cr distribution in control samples causes slower or incomplete passivation.
Control samples are more susceptible to corrosion because of their heterogeneous Cr distribution.
The proposed mechanism applies to high-chromium steels in oxidative corrosive environments typical of chemical-processing and nuclear-power service.
The proposed mechanism may not apply to low-chromium alloys or non-oxidizing environments.
Electron diffraction or atom-probe tomography can be used to assess short-range ordering.
Potentiodynamic polarization and weight-loss testing can be used to evaluate corrosion rate.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis and mechanism describe ordering as homogenizing Cr, whereas the structural mediator is explicitly Cr-rich nanoclusters, which implies nanoscale Cr heterogeneity. The relationship between clustering and greater uniformity is not reconciled.
